public.prompt: A cell in the Orders sheet displays the text "Lagos". Which of the following best describes the difference between the cell's address and its contents?

options.text: The address is the column-letter/row-number label (e.g., B2) that identifies where the cell sits in the grid; the contents are the value stored inside it (e.g., "Lagos").
The address is the value stored in the cell (e.g., "Lagos"); the column letter and row number are just display labels.
The address and the contents are the same thing — both refer to the text "Lagos" shown in the cell.
The address is the row number only (e.g., 2); the column letter is part of the contents.

opt_b.message: That is reversed. The value "Lagos" is the cell's contents — what is stored inside it. The address is the column-letter/row-number label (like B2) that tells you where the cell lives in the grid.

opt_c.message: They are different things. The address (e.g., B2) is a fixed location label; the contents (e.g., "Lagos") are what you typed or calculated. You could change the contents without changing the address.

opt_d.message: A cell address includes both the column letter and the row number together (e.g., B2). Neither part alone is the address, and neither is part of the contents.

correct.message: Exactly right. The address (B2) is the fixed grid location; the contents ("Lagos") are the value stored there. You can change the contents without changing the address.

incorrect.message: The address is the column-letter/row-number label that locates the cell in the grid (e.g., B2). The contents are the value stored inside that cell (e.g., "Lagos"). They are two separate things.

hints: Think about what stays the same when you type something new into a cell — the location label or the value?
In Excel, the Name Box (top-left) shows the address; the cell itself shows the contents.

public.prompt: The QuickDeliver workbook has a sheet named Orders. In that sheet, column B holds the delivery city and row 2 holds the first order. Type a formula in cell A1 that returns the value stored at the intersection of column B and row 2.

correct.message: Correct! =B2 points at column B, row 2 — the first order's city in the Orders sheet. The address B2 is the column letter followed by the row number, exactly as the A1 reference style works.

incorrect.message: Remember: a cell address is the column letter followed by the row number. Column B, row 2 gives the address B2. Type =B2 to return the value stored there.

hints: The column letter comes first, then the row number — no space between them.
Start your formula with = so Excel knows it is a formula, not plain text.

public.prompt: New delivery orders are added to the Orders sheet every day, so the city column keeps growing. Which reference covers every cell in column B, no matter how many rows are added?

opt_b.message: B2:B51 covers only rows 2 through 51. If a 52nd order is added, that row is outside the range. A whole-column reference like B:B always covers every row, past and future.

opt_c.message: B1 is a single-cell reference — it points at just one cell, the header row. It does not cover the rest of column B.

opt_d.message: B:2 is not valid range notation. A whole-column reference repeats the column letter on both sides of the colon: B:B. A whole-row reference repeats the row number: 2:2.

correct.message: Correct! B:B selects every cell in column B by repeating the column letter on both sides of the colon. It automatically includes any new rows added later.

incorrect.message: To reference an entire column, repeat the column letter on both sides of a colon: B:B. This covers every row in column B, including rows added in the future.

hints: A whole-column reference uses the same letter twice, separated by a colon.
Compare: 5:5 selects all of row 5; the same pattern with a letter selects all of a column.

public.prompt: The Orders sheet has 20 orders in rows 2 through 21. The delivery_minutes values are in column C. The range C2:C21 covers all the delivery_minutes values. In cell A1, type a formula that returns the value from the first cell in this range (the delivery_minutes value for the first order in row 2).

correct.message: Correct! =C2 references the first cell in the range C2:C21. A range reference like C2:C21 uses a colon to connect the starting cell (C2) and the ending cell (C21), covering all cells in between.

incorrect.message: The range C2:C21 starts at cell C2 (column C, row 2) and ends at C21 (column C, row 21). To reference the first cell in this range, type =C2.

hints: A range reference uses a colon between two cell addresses: start:end. The range C2:C21 starts at C2.
The first cell in a range is the cell address that appears before the colon.
